ལ། གཟུགས་བརྙན་དུ་སྣང་བ་ནི་སྤྲུལ་པ་ཙམ་སྟེ། སྤྲུལ་པ་ཉིད་རྐྱེན་སྣང་གློ་བུར་བ་ཡིན་ཏེ། སྐྱེ་མེད་ཀྱི་དབྱིངས་ལ་སྤྲུལ་པ་དང་། གློ་བུར་བ་ཙམ་དུ་ཡང་མ་གྲུབ་ཅིང་མ་སྐྱེས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །སྣང་བ་འདི་གསལ་བ་དང་པོ་ཉིད་ནས་མ་སྐྱེས་ཏེ། སྐྱེ་མེད་ཀྱི་དབྱིངས་ཉིད་
བརྗོད་དུ་མ་བཏུབ་པས། བློ་ལས་འདས་ཏེ་བློ་ལས་འདས་པ་ཉིད་ཕྱག་རྒྱ་ཆེན་པོའོ། །དེ་ལ་མཚན་ཉིད་བཞི་དང་ལྡན་ཏེ་ཀུན་ལ་ཁྱབ་པ། གཟུགས་ཅན་མ་ཡིན་པ་འགྲོ་འོང་མེད་པ། དུས་ཐམས་ཅད་པ་སྟེ། ཀུན་ལ་ཁྱབ་པ་ནི་ཀུན་གྱི་དངོས་གཞི་ཡིན་ཏེ། འཁོར་བ་
དང་མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པ་དང་། རྒྱུ་དང་འབྲས་བུ་དང་སྣང་བ་དང་སྟོང་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་ལ་ཁྱབ་པའོ། །གཟུགས་ཅན་མ་ཡིན་པ་ནི། རྟེན་ཅིང་འབྲེལ་པའམ། རྐྱེན་གྱིས་བསྐྱེད་ནས་ཕུང་པོ་དང་ཁམས་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་སྣང་ཡང་ངོས་བཟུང་

མོ་གཤམ་གྱི་བུ་ལྟར་ཆད་པའམ་མེད་པ་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་དང་སྙིང་རྗེ་དབྱེར་མེད་པར། །མ་ཧཱ་མུ་དྲ་དེ་དུས་ཐམས་ཅད་དུ་གནས་པའོ། །དེའི་ཕྱིར་གཟུགས་ཅན་མ་ཡིན་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་རྣམ་པར་སྤངས། མ་ཧཱ་མུ་དྲ་དེ་དུས་རྒྱུན་དུ་ས་མ་ཏི་བཞིའི་ཚུལ་དུ་གནས་

The <term>dharmata</term> <gloss>intrinsic nature of reality</gloss> is not produced by circumstances; it has never experienced birth, never experienced cessation, and never experienced being known. Although this appearance arises within its nature, it appears only like a reflection in a mirror, for the mirror has no conceptual thought of the reflection arising within it. The mirror is like the <term>dhatu</term> <gloss>sphere or dimension</gloss> of non-birth, and what appears as a reflection is merely an emanation. This very emanation is a sudden, circumstantial appearance; yet, within the dimension of non-birth, even emanation and suddenness are not established and have not been born.

From the very first, this clarity of appearance has not been born. Because the dimension of non-birth cannot be expressed, it transcends the intellect. This very state of transcending the intellect is <term>Mahamudra</term> <gloss>the Great Seal</gloss>. It possesses four characteristics: it is all-pervasive, it is non-material, it is without coming and going, and it is timeless.

Regarding its all-pervasiveness: it is the basic foundation of everything. It pervades all of <term>samsara</term> <gloss>cyclic existence</gloss> and <term>nirvana</term> <gloss>liberation</gloss>, cause and effect, appearance and emptiness, and so forth.

Regarding its being non-material: although all phenomena such as the <term>skandhas</term> <gloss>aggregates</gloss> and <term>dhatus</term> <gloss>elements</gloss> appear through dependent origination or are produced by circumstances, they are devoid of any identifiable identity; they are unborn by nature.

Regarding its being without coming and going: because there is no birth or cessation, all is pervaded by the nature of reality. It is not occasional; everything is the very nature of <term>tathata</term> <gloss>suchness</gloss>.

Regarding its being timeless: <term>Mahamudra</term> <gloss>the Great Seal</gloss> is not something that is terminated or non-existent like a rabbit's horn or the son of a barren woman. <term>Mahamudra</term> exists at all times as the inseparability of emptiness and compassion.

Therefore, being non-material, it is utterly free from the nature of physical form. This <term>Mahamudra</term> remains constantly in the manner of the four <term>samadhis</term> <gloss>meditative absorptions</gloss>. By practicing <term>dhyana</term> <gloss>meditative concentration</gloss> continuously, without anything to meditate upon and without distraction, that very state remains constantly as a single concentration. Any meditation that involves an object of meditation or mental effort is stained; it is not the ultimate mind.

<summary>This page defines Mahamudra through the analogy of a mirror and reflection, emphasizing its unborn nature. It outlines four essential characteristics of the Great Seal: all-pervasiveness, non-materiality, lack of motion, and timelessness.</summary>

གསུངས་པ་དེ་དག་ཀྱང་། གཉིས་མེད་ཀྱི་རྣལ་འབྱོར་དུ་བྱ་བའི་བརྡར་གསུངས་པ་ནི། རྒྱལ་པོ་རྣམས་ནི་རིན་ཆེན་སྐལ་བར་ལྡན། །སྨན་པ་བཟང་དང་ཕྲད་པར་གྱུར་པ་ལས། །ཉི་མའི་དཀྱིལ་འཁོར་མུན་པ་སེལ་བ་ལྟར། །རུས་སྦལ་རྒྱ་མཚོ་དག་ཏུ་འགྲོ་མི་འགྱུར། །
སྟོབས་ལྡན་གྱད་ཀྱིས་ཕ་རོལ་འཇོམས་པར་བྱེད། །རི་བོ་འགྱེལ་ན་ཆུ་རྣམས་འབྲུབ་པར་བྱེད། །ནགས་ཁྲོད་དག་ན་རྔོན་པ་གླུ་རྣམས་ལེན། །མེ་ཤེལ་རས་བལ་འདུས་པས་མེ་འབྱུང་འགྱུར། །གསེར་འགྱུར་རྩི་ནི་ཤིན་ཏུ་ངོ་མཚར་ཆེ། །ཆུ་དང་བཅས་པའི་སྐྱེ་ཤིང་
ལོ་འདབ་རྒྱས། །སྦུར་ལེན་ནོར་བུ་དག་ནི་སྦུར་རྣམས་སྡུད། །ཤེས་པ་རྣམས་ནི་གཞན་གྱི་ལུས་ལ་འཇུག །སྤྲེའུ་རྣམས་ནི་དྲན་པར་ལྡན་པ་སྟེ། །མཉན་པས་འགྲོ་བ་དག་ནི་སྒྲོལ་བར་བྱེད། །ག་བུར་སྦྱོར་བས་ཚད་པའི་ནད་རྣམས་སེལ། །དགེ་སློང་བག་དང་ལྡན་པ་

<meta>This text is a translation of a section from the Derge Tengyur, specifically a commentary on esoteric instructions involving symbolic codes or ciphers used in Vajrayana Buddhism.</meta>

It is said:
Entirely pure without an interior; refined gold is free from the tarnish of impurities.

This constitutes the fifth instruction for severing the distress of the natural state of the fruit <note>the final result or realization</note>.

Regarding what the <term>Dakini</term> <gloss>sky-goer; female wisdom deity</gloss> Maha taught to the Master Dombi Heruka, those words were spoken as symbols for practicing non-dual yoga:

Kings possess a share of jewels.
Upon meeting a good physician,
Just as the solar mandala dispels darkness,
A turtle will not go into the Great Ocean.
A powerful athlete subdues the opponent.
When a mountain collapses, the waters overflow.
In the forest depths, the hunter sings songs.
When a burning lens <note>a crystal or magnifying glass</note> meets cotton, fire is produced.
The alchemy of gold-making is a supreme wonder.
Living trees with water flourish with leaves and foliage.
Amber stones <note>literally "straw-attractor" jewels</note> gather up the straw.
The conscious ones enter the bodies of others.
Monkeys are endowed with mindfulness.
By listening, beings are liberated.
By applying camphor, the diseases of heat are cleared.
The disciplined monk performs the <term>Sojong</term> <gloss>confession and purification ritual</gloss>.
The low-born does not reside in the King’s palace.
If cut, the palm tree has no leaves.
The illusionist is skilled in the enjoyments of illusion.
The King’s daughter is perfectly adorned with ornaments.
Dancers perform the various forms of the dance.
Bees rush into the midst of vomit.

These are the sixth instructions for severing the distress of the natural state of non-dual yoga.

Next, the <term>Dakini</term> Beto spoke the symbols of the yoga of union to the Guru from Zanglingpa <note>the Copper Isle</note> at Kappura:

The throne of the heart is endowed with compassion;
A mother is deeply attached to her son.
Just as molasses comes from the sugarcane,
By going to the ocean, the jewel is found.
One does not remove the moon from within the water.
The fire-crystal jewel is free from striving and achievement.
The King's consort...

<summary>This page details symbolic instructions or ciphers given by Dakinis to great masters like Dombi Heruka, using natural metaphors to explain the non-dual state of yoga. It concludes by beginning a new set of instructions concerning the yoga of union transmitted to the Guru of Zanglingpa.</summary>
<keywords>Dombi Heruka, Dakini, non-dual yoga, alchemy, symbols, Vajrayana, Zanglingpa</keywords>

Never having been born from the very beginning,
The wise understand that the mind has no cessation.
There is no need to meditate on specific antidotes <note>remedies or counter-measures for negative emotions</note>.
The yogi should look inward.
Since there is no experience except from the mind,
Regarding the appearance and existence of the permanent and impermanent,
There is neither negation nor affirmation.
If you know that the mind itself is <term>Jnana</term> <gloss>primordial wisdom</gloss>,
Then there is no need to demonstrate <term>Nirvana</term> <gloss>the state beyond suffering</gloss>.
Even if attachment and aversion arise,
The antidotes such as contemplating the unattractive <note>a meditation to counter lust</note> or loving-kindness
Do not reside as two separate things in the mental continuum of beings.
Just as various clouds
Dissolve into the expanse of the sky,
When things, together with adventitious <note>temporary or incidental</note> luminosity,
Later cease within their own nature,
Upon whom would one meditate on an antidote?
When the habitual tendencies of ignorant delusion
Appear to the mind like a mirage,
To meditate on an antidote is as wondrously strange
As an unskilled person trying to "fix" a mirage.
The nature of the mind is luminosity;
If birth itself is not stable,
How could adventitious factors be permanent?
Therefore, do not meditate on antidotes;
There are no antidotes, and there is no meditation.
The yogi who does not grasp at signs <note>conceptual characteristics</note>
Does not think of this or that.
There is no waning and no cessation.
Non-composite, it is like the sky.
The faults of <term>Samadhi</term> <gloss>meditative absorption</gloss> arise from perception.
There is no thought of "I am not composing."
By prolonging the state free from concepts in direct perception,
One applies the conventional term "meditation."
Even though non-conceptuality is born from the beginning,
The clearing away of exaggerations <note>superimpositions or mental constructs</note> is meditation.
If one does not allow the unconditioned self-clarity to be,
Then even if one forcefully meditates on non-conceptuality,
Non-conceptuality itself becomes a cause of obscuration.
For example, if medicine itself is not digested,
It becomes the heaviest of illnesses.
Effortless meditation is called "cutting through exaggerations."
If one does not know things to be like an illusion or the moon in water,
Merely saying "empty" will not enter the mind at all.
If the nature of the mind is realized as appearance-emptiness,
Compassion for beings arises naturally.
When the mind arises seeing no distinction between self and others,
Like the moon in water,
That is called the "meditation of great bliss."

<summary>This text explains that because the mind's nature is primordial wisdom and inherently empty, forceful meditation and artificial antidotes for emotions are unnecessary. It emphasizes realizing the mind as effortless luminosity and the unity of appearance and emptiness to foster natural compassion.</summary>
<keywords>primordial wisdom, non-conceptuality, luminosity, emptiness, meditation, antidotes, compassion, Great Bliss</keywords>

ཚོགས། །སྐད་ཅིག་བཞི་ཡིས་དགའ་བ་གསུམ་སོན་འབྲིང་པོའི་དྲོད་དེ་ལྷན་ཅིག་སྐྱེས་པ་དྷཱུ་ཏཱིའི་ལམ་ཞུགས་ནས། །འཇིག་རྟེན་ལས་འདས་བརྒྱ་ཕྲག་བདུན་པོ་ཡོན་ཏན་གྱིས་སྤྲས་གནས་དང་ཉེ་གནས་ཉི་ཤུ་བཞི་ལ་སོགས། །དངས་མ་ཡས་བྱོན་པཱུལླི་སོགས་ཁྱབ་རྒྱུ་བ་མས་བརྟན་བདེ་ཆེན་
བརྟོལ་ནས་མ་ཆགས་པདྨའི་ས། །རབ་བཀྲམ་ཆེན་པོ་ཕྲག་བདུན་ཡོན་ཏན་ཡེ་ཤེས་གསལ་བྱེད་ཆོས་སྐུ་བདག་ཉིད་རྡོ་རྗེ་འཛིན་པར་འགྱུར། །འཁོར་ལོ་སྡོམ་པའི་བསྐྱེད་རྫོགས་ལ་སོགས་གཏིང་དཔག་དཀའ་བ་གསལ་པོར་རབ་ཕྱེ་སྙན་བརྒྱུད་མཁའ་འགྲོའི་གསང་། །དྲི་མེད་བསགས་
པའི་དགེ་བ་དེས་ནི་ས་གསུམ་གནས་པ་རྡོ་རྗེ་འཛིན་པའི་གོ་འཕང་ཐོབ་པར་ཤོག །ཡིད་བཞིན་ནོར་བུ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་མཁའ་འགྲོ་མའི་གསང་ཚིག་ཏིལླི་པས་བཀོད་པ་རྫོགས་སོ།། །།རྩིགས་ཀྱི་རྒྱ་མདུད་དང་བཅས་པ་ནཱ་རོ་པཎྜི་ཏའི་ཞལ་སྔ་ནས་དང་། ལོ་ཙཱ་བ་མར་པ་ཆོས་
ཀྱི་བློ་གྲོས་ཀྱིས་པུཥྤ་ཧ་རིའི་གནས་སུ་བསྒྱུར་བའོ།། {D2338}༄༅༅། །རྒྱ་གར་སྐད་དུ། ཀཪྞ་ཏནྟྲ་བཛྲ་པ་ད་ནཱ་མ། བོད་སྐད་དུ། སྙན་བརྒྱུད་རྡོ་རྗེའི་ཚིག་རྐང་ཞེས་བྱ་བ། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་དཔལ་རྡོ་རྗེ་འཆང་ལ་ཕྱག་འཚལ་ལོ། །ཨེ་མ་ཧོ། སངས་རྒྱས་
ཀུན་གྱི་ཡང་དག་གསང་བའི་མཆོག །ཡེ་ཤེས་རྒྱལ་པོ་ཐིག་ལེ་མཆོག་གི་ལམ། །ཚིག་ཏུ་བརྗོད་པ་ཀུན་དང་བྲལ་བའི་དོན། །ཐེག་ཆེན་སྐྱེ་མེད་རང་སྒྲ་འདི་སྐད་ཐོས། །རྡོ་རྗེ་འཆང་ངས་སྐལ་ལྡན་དོན་དུ་བཤད། །གུས་བཏུད་ནས་ནི་ཡེ་ཤེས་མཁའ་འགྲོ་ཉོན། །བསླབ་

Burning the firewood <note>referring to the dissolution of dualistic thoughts and physical aggregates</note>, one is liberated into the luminous <term>Dharmakaya</term> <gloss>Truth Body</gloss>. To receive this meaning through the successive lineage, one must rely on the Guru with devotion. Thus, the oral transmission of the "Carrying the Blessings onto the Path" was passed from ear to ear. Those of supreme intellect, motivated by great compassion, abandon other vehicles and strive in the two stages of ripening <note>the Generation Stage</note> and liberation <note>the Completion Stage</note>. By purifying the environment and its inhabitants as the divine palace, and the aggregates and elements as deities, all Victors <note>Buddhas</note> are gathered within.

Since Great Bliss resides in the <term>vajra</term> <gloss>adamantine</gloss> body, the messengers <note>yogic energies or consorts</note> and the elaborated or unelaborated wheels are brought into union. Through stable devotion to these stages, emanations are perceived; because the faults and virtues are small, they are gathered. Through the four moments, the three joys are attained; this is the "warmth" of the intermediate practitioner. Entering the path of the <term>dhuti</term> <gloss>central channel</gloss>, one transcends the world, adorned with seven hundred qualities.

From the twenty-four sacred sites and minor sites, the pure essence descends from above through places like <term>Pulliramale</term>. Moving and stabilizing from below, one pierces Great Bliss and reaches the stage of the unattached Lotus. The seven hundred great qualities clarify primordial wisdom; one becomes the <term>Vajradhara</term> <gloss>Vajra Holder</gloss>, the very nature of the Truth Body. These profound and difficult points of the generation and completion stages of <term>Chakrasamvara</term> have been clearly opened—the secret of the <term>Dakinis</term> <gloss>sky-goers</gloss> of the oral transmission. By the merit of accumulating these stainless teachings, may all beings in the three realms attain the rank of a Vajra Holder.

This concludes the "Wish-Fulfilling Jewel," the secret words of the Dakinis composed by <term>Tillipa</term> <gloss>Tilopa</gloss>. It was received from the presence of the scholar <term>Naropa</term> and translated at the <term>Pushpahari</term> monastery by the translator <term>Marpa Chokyi Lodro</term>.

In the language of India: <term>Karnatantra Vajrapada Nama</term>
In the language of Tibet: <term>Snyan brgyud rdo rje'i tshig rkang zhes bya ba</term> <gloss>The Vajra Verses of the Oral Transmission</gloss>

Homage to the Blessed Lord, Glorious <term>Vajradhara</term>.

<term>Emaho</term> <gloss>An exclamation of wonder</gloss>! The authentic, supreme secret of all Buddhas, the path of the supreme <term>thigle</term> <gloss>seminal drop</gloss>, the King of Primordial Wisdom. This meaning is free from all verbal expression. This self-arisen sound of the unborn Great Vehicle was heard thus: I, Vajradhara, shall explain it for the sake of the fortunate. Listen, Wisdom Dakini, having bowed with devotion...

<summary>This page concludes Tilopa's Wish-Fulfilling Jewel and begins the Vajra Verses of the Oral Transmission, a foundational text of the Kagyu lineage detailing the path of Great Bliss and the central channel.</summary>

སྣམ་བུ་དང་བྲལ་བའི་ཕྱིར་འདི་དག་ནི་སྣལ་མའོ་འདི་ནི་སྣམ་བུའོ་ཞེས་རྟོགས་པ་ཇི་ལྟར་འགྱུར་ཞེ་ན། དེ་ནི་བདེན་པ་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ་གང་གི་ཕྱིར། འགའ་ཞིག་སྒྲ་རྟེན་སྟོན་པ་ན། །རྒྱུ་རུ་ཉེ་བར་འདོགས་པ་འམ། །སྣལ་མ་གཅིག་ནི་གསེས་ནས་ཀྱང་། །འབྲས་ལ་སྣལ་མ་ཞེས་འཇུག་འགྱུར། །ཞེས་བྱ་བ་
ལ། སྣལ་མའི་འབྲས་བུ་ནི་སྣམ་བུ་ཉིད་དེ་དེའི་ཚེ་སྣལ་མ་མེད་དོ། །སྔར་སྣལ་མ་རྒྱུ་ཡིན་པས་བཏགས་ནས་སྣལ་མའི་ཤེས་པ་དང་སྣལ་མའི་སྒྲ་འབྲས་བུ་སྣམ་བུ་ལ་སྐྱེའོ། །འཇུག་པར་འགྱུར་ཏེ་འདི་ལྟར་སྔར་གྱི་སྣལ་མ་དྲན་ནས་འདི་དག་སྣལ་མའོ་ཞེས་རྟོགས་ཀྱི་གཞན་དུ་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །སྣལ་
མ་རེ་རེ་ནས་གསེས་ནས་ཀྱང་སྣལ་མའོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བར་འཇུག་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །ཅི་ཞིག་བྱ་ཞེ་ན། སྣམ་བུ་ལ། སྣལ་མའི་སྒྲའི་རྟེན་བསྟན་པར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་ཏེ། འདི་ལྟར་སྣལ་མ་དེ་ཉིད་བསྡུས་ནས་ཁྱད་པར་ཅན་གྱི་དུས་སུ་སོན་པ་ན་སྣམ་བུ་ཞེས་བརྗོད་དོ། །དེའི་ཕྱིར་དམག་དང་ནགས་བཞིན་དུ་སྣམ་བུ་
ནི་ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཏུ་ཡོད་པ་ཉིད་ཡིན་གྱི། དོན་དམ་པར་སྣལ་མ་ལས་ཐ་དད་པའི་སྣམ་བུ་ཡོད་པ་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །འོ་ན་གལ་ཏེ་སྣལ་མ་ལས་ཐ་དད་པའི་སྣམ་བུ་མེད་ན་ཇི་ལྟར་སྣམ་བུའི་སྒྲ་འཇུག་པར་འགྱུར་ཏེ། ཕྱི་རོལ་གྱི་རྒྱུ་མཚན་མེད་པར་བརྗོད་པས་འཇུག་པར་ནུས་པ་མ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ་ཞེ་ན། 
དེ་ནི་རིགས་པ་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ་གང་གི་ཕྱིར། ཕན་གདགས་ཕན་འདོགས་བྱེད་ཉིད་དམ། །རིས་ཆད་མཐོང་བ་མེད་པ་ཉིད། །ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ལ། སྣམ་བུའི་སྒྲའི་རྒྱུ་མཚན་ཡིན་པར་བལྟ་བར་བྱའོ། །ཐ་ག་པ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་གྲོགས་བྱེད་པས་ཕུལ་དུ་བྱུང་བ་ཅན་གྱི་སྣལ་མ་རྣམས་ཕན་ཚུན་ཕན་གདགས་པར་བྱ་

If one asks: since the wool <note>original: "snam bu"</note> is distinct from the threads <note>original: "snal ma"</note>, how is it that one perceives them as "these are the threads" and "this is the wool"?

That is not true, because:

When someone indicates the basis of a word,
It is either a metaphorical attribution to the cause,
Or even after separating a single thread,
The term "thread" is applied to the result.

Regarding this: the result of the threads is the wool itself; at that time, the threads <note>as independent entities</note> no longer exist. Because the threads were previously the cause, by way of attribution, the cognition of "threads" and the word "thread" arise for the result, which is the wool. This application occurs in this way: by remembering the previous threads, one perceives "these are the threads," but not otherwise. Even after separating each thread one by one, the application of the term "thread" occurs.

If one asks: what is the purpose? It is for the sake of showing the basis for the word "thread" in relation to the wool. Thus, when those very threads are gathered and reach a specific state, it is called "wool." Therefore, just like a "army" or a "forest," the "wool" exists only as a conventional reality <note>original: "kun rdzob tu yod pa"</note>; in ultimate reality <note>original: "don dam par"</note>, there is no wool that exists as something separate from the threads.

Now, if one objects: if there is no wool separate from the threads, how can the word "wool" be applied? For without an external objective reason, a verbal expression cannot be applied.

That is not logical, because:

The state of being benefited and benefactor,
Or the fact that no distinction is seen.

Regarding this: these should be viewed as the reasons for the word "wool." The threads, having been made excellent through the assistance of the weaver and so forth, act as that which is benefited and that which benefits one another. Because that very relationship is the cause of the word "wool," the fact that the threads themselves exist in a state of being benefited and benefactor to accomplish purposes such as clothing is the reason for the word "wool."

Alternatively, the fact that no distinction is seen among the threads is the cause for the conventional term "wool." For example, if the assistance of the weaving <note>original: "thag bzang"</note> and so forth were absent, the threads would be separated and carried away individually. However, at the time of being "wool," that is not the case; therefore, the absence of seeing a distinction is the cause for the word, just as it is for the word "pot"…

<summary>This page discusses the relationship between a whole and its parts using the analogy of wool and threads. It argues that the "whole" is a conventional designation based on the causal relationship and arrangement of its parts rather than a separate ultimate entity.</summary>
<keywords>mereology, whole and parts, conventional reality, ultimate reality, linguistics, causal attribution, weaver analogy</keywords>

མེད་པ་ཉིད་ཡིན་ན་ཡང་། སྦྱངས་པ་ངེས་པས་ངེས་པའི་(དེན་,དོན་)མཐོང་བ་ལས་སྐྱེས་ནས་སོ་སོར་ངེས་པ་དྲན་པར་བྱེད་དེ། རང་ཉིད་ངེས་པར་གྱུར་ནའོ། །དོན་ངེས་པར་མཐོང་བ་ནི་རྣམ་པ་མེད་ན་གྲུབ་པ་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། ངེས་པར་མཐོང་བ་མེད་ན་ཡང་འདུ་བྱེད་པ་མ་ཡིན་ལ། དེ་མེད་ན་ཡང་ངེས་པ་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །གལ་
ཏེ་བྱ་བྱེད་གཅིག་ཡིན་པར། །འགལ་ལོ་ཞེ་ན་མི་བདེན་ཏེ། ཆོས་ཐ་དད་པར་ཁས་ལེན་ཕྱིར། །དངོས་པོ་ཐ་དད་མེད་པར་འདོད། །ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི། འོ་ན་གལ་ཏེ་ཤེས་པའི་རྣམ་པ་ཚད་མ་ཡིན་ལ། དོན་རྟོགས་པ་འབྲས་བུ་ཡིན་ན་ནི། །དེ་ལྟ་ན་ཡང་བྱ་བ་དང་བྱེད་པ་དེ་དག་གཅིག་པར་འགྱུར་ན། དེ་ནི་

All boundaries and details will be seen, but this is not the appearance of a mere collection or aggregate. For this reason, the distinction between proximity and distance in seeing a tree reveals appearances that are either clear or unclear. To show that the very nature of this clarity or lack of clarity in the external body is the <term>pramana</term> <gloss>valid cognition or means of knowledge</gloss>, the text says:

Although it is indivisible, this distinction
Exists from whatever source; that itself is the valid cognition.

Regarding this, even though the encounter <note>the meeting of the faculty and the object</note> is indivisible, the distinction between clear and unclear aspects of this realization is established. Whatever source establishes this is correctly identified as the valid cognition itself.

If it arises from a refinement, the appearance therein
Does not exist, and cannot be established as such.

This means: What if one argues that even a consciousness without any mental aspect <note>original: "nirakara," referring to the theory that consciousness does not take on the form of the object</note> could distinguish between different objects through a specific conditioned refinement? That is not logical, because such a status cannot be established through mere refinement. Even if that consciousness lacked a reflected appearance—meaning it was without a mental aspect—the memory of specific determinations would only arise from seeing a determined object through a specific refinement, provided that one is themselves certain. Seeing an object with certainty cannot be achieved if there is no mental aspect. If there is no certain seeing, there is no mental formation, and without that, there is no certainty.

If it is argued that the act and the agent being one
Is a contradiction, that is untrue;
Because we accept different qualities,
While asserting there is no difference in the entity.

This means: Well, if the mental aspect of consciousness is the valid cognition and the realization of the object is the result, then the act and the agent would become one and the same. This would be a contradiction, as a sickle cannot cut itself. However, that argument is untrue. This is because the qualities, such as the mental aspects, differ without the consciousness itself being separate. That which is excluded from being non-aspected is the consciousness possessing a mental aspect; that which is excluded from being non-realized is the nature of realization. These are the same entity. We assert they are inseparable in the definition of consciousness. Without the mental aspect of blue and so forth, there would be no experience of blue. Since the experience itself lacks anything other than blue, the "blueness" and the consciousness are identical. We see the act and the agent as distinct only in terms of their functional properties.

<summary>This page discusses Buddhist epistemology and the relationship between consciousness and its mental aspects, arguing that valid cognition and its result are identical in entity but conceptually distinct.</summary>
<keywords>valid cognition, pramana, mental aspect, consciousness, non-dualism, Buddhist logic, perception</keywords>

ཡོད་པ་དེ་ཉིད་ལ་དེ་ལས་འབྱུང་བའི་སྡུག་བསྔལ་ལ་སོགས་པ་སྐྱེ་བའི་རྣལ་འབྱོར་པ་ལ་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེ་ན། དེ་ནི་མི་བདེན་ཏེ། འདི་ལྟར། སྡུག་བསྔལ་ཀུན་ནས་འབྱུང་བ་དག། །སྡུག་བསྔལ་མྱོང་མིན་འོན་ཀྱང་ནི། །སྡུག་བསྔལ་ཤེས་པ་འབྱུང་བ་ཡིན། །སྡུག་བསྔལ་ལ་སོགས་མ་མྱོང་བ། །

ཁས་ལེན་པའི་ཚེ་རྣལ་འབྱོར་པ་གཞན་གྱི་སྡུག་བསྔལ་རིག་པ་ཡིན་ཡང་ནད་པར་ཐལ་འགྱུར་བ་ནི་མེད་དེ། འདི་ལྟར་སྐམ་ལ་གནས་པ་ཆུ་ལ་དམིགས་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་བཞིན་བདེ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ལ་དམིགས་པ་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཁྱེད་ཀྱི་ལུགས་ཀྱིས་ན་སྐམ་ལ་གནས་པ་བཞིན་བདེ་བ་

The phrase <note>from the source text</note> states: However, because there is no object, such as the woman Bhadra and so forth, nor is there a meeting <gloss>contact or union</gloss>, those yogis do not experience the pleasure or pain that arises from the meeting of objects and the senses. If one asks, "Is it not the case that only worldly beings, who possess the meeting of objects and the senses, experience the resulting suffering and so forth, while yogis do not?" that is not true. For this reason, it is said:

The arising of suffering
Is not the experience of suffering; rather,
It is the emergence of the cognition of suffering.
What does not experience suffering and so forth
Is not the cause of affliction or benefit.

Regarding this: the mere arising of suffering does not constitute having the experience of suffering. If one asks, "What is it then?" it is the experience of suffering becoming manifest that causes affliction. For example, is it not seen that common pleasure, such as the bristling of body hair <note>goosebumps</note>, is produced from the contact of the tactile senses with human women? Therefore, if it is experienced, it becomes pleasure, but it is not pleasure by its mere arising. Because if it does not appear to oneself as suffering and so forth, it is not the cause of affliction or benefit.

If one asks, "Do not Buddhist yogis also cognize the suffering of others? How then do they not become afflicted?" the text states:

When one is suffering oneself,
The appearance of its own nature is affliction.
The cognition that observes that is not like that;
At that time, there is no such consequence.

When suffering has arisen to be experienced by its own nature, one accepts being afflicted or not afflicted; at that time, it becomes suffering. However, one is not afflicted by mere cognition directed toward the three types of suffering. Thus, when accepting this, even though a yogis cognizes the suffering of others, there is no consequence of them becoming ill. This is like someone staying on dry land observing water and so forth; it is not the same as observing pleasure and so forth <note>from within the experience</note>. <summary>This page discusses the Buddhist philosophical distinction between the mere arising of suffering and the actual experience or cognition of it. It argues that yogis can perceive the suffering of others without being afflicted by it themselves, using the analogy of a person on dry land observing water.</summary>

བྱེད་ཀྱི་ཡང་ཡིན་ནོ། །དེས་ན་རིག་བྱེད་ལ་ཡང་བྱེད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། ཚད་མ་ལ་ལྟོས་གཞོན་ནུ་འབྱུང་བ་ཅན་ལ་སོགས་པ་བཞིན་ནོ། །ཁྱབ་པ་ཇི་ལྟར་ཞེ་ན། རིགས་གང་གང་ལས་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཚུལ་ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །བརྗོད་དཀའ་བ་དང་མཉན་དཀའ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་
དང་། དུག་སེལ་བར་བྱེད་པ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ནུས་པའི་ཁྱད་པར་རམ། དབང་པོ་ལས་འདས་པའི་དོན་སྟོན་པར་བྱེད་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་རིགས་མི་གཅིག་པར་བརྟག་པར་བྱ་བ་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེ་དག་ཀྱང་ཐམས་ཅད་དང་ཐུན་མོང་བ་ཉིད་དོ། །དེ་ལ་ལྟོས་ནས་བཤད་པ་ནི་ཡང་ན་དེ་
དང་ཁྱད་པར་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་སྟེ། རིག་བྱེད་དང་ཁྱད་པར་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དེ་ལྟ་ཡིན་དང་ཚིག་སོ་སོར་ངེས་པའི་ཚད་མ་མེད་པས་ན། རིག་བྱེད་ཀྱི་ཚད་མ་འབའ་ཞིག་ཚད་མར་ཁས་མི་བླང་ངོ་སྙམ་དུ་དགོངས་པའོ། །སྐྱེས་བུས་བྱས་པས་ཞེས་
བྱ་བ་ནི་གཞན་གྱིས་དོགས་པའོ། །ཁྱབ་འཇུག་གི་ལུང་ལ་སོགས་པ་ནི་སྐྱེས་བུས་བྱས་པར་གྲགས་པས་ན། དེ་ནི་སྐྱེས་བུས་མ་བྱས་པ་ལ་གནོད་དོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །སྐྱེས་བུ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ནི་སུན་འབྱིན་པར་བྱེད་པའོ། །རིག་བྱེད་ལ་ཡང་མ་རྟོགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་
ན་སྐྱེས་བུས་བྱས་པ་མ་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེས་བརྗོད་པར་མི་བྱ་སྟེ། འདས་ནས་ཤིན་ཏུ་ཡུན་རིང་དུ་ལོན་ནས་དབང་པོ་ལས་འདས་པའི་ཕྱིར་མ་དམིགས་ཀྱང་བྱེད་པ་པོ་དགག་པར་མི་ནུས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དེས་ན་བྱེད་པ་པོ་མེད་པ་ཉིད་ཐེ་ཚོམ་ཟའོ། །དེ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཕྱིར་སྐྱེས་བུས་བྱས་པ་དེ་སྐྱེས་བུས་
མ་བྱས་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་གནོད་བྱེད་མ་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་འདི་ཚད་མ་ག་ལས་ཡིན་ཏེ། ཚད་མ་འགའ་ཡང་ཡོད་པ་མ་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །རྩོད་པ་འདི་ནི་ལེའུ་དང་པོར་སྤྲོས་པ་ཡིན་ལ། འདིར་ནི་སྐབས་ཀྱིས་ཅུང་ཟད་བརྗོད་པར་ཟད་དོ། །ཕྱོགས་གཞན་བརྗོད་པ་ནི་ཡང་ན་ཞེས་བྱ་
བའོ། །ཚིག་དེ་ནི་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་གང་ལ་བྱེད་པ་པོ་ཡོད་པར་གྲགས་པའོ། །གང་གིས་འདི་ལྟར་བརྗོད་པ་རང་གིས་མ་བྱས་པར་བདག་གིས་བྱས་སོ་སྙམ་པར་འཁྲུལ་པ་མཐོང་བ་ཡོད་དམ་སྙམ་དུ་དོགས་ན། འདི་ལྟར་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པའོ། །རློམ་པར་འགྱུར་བ་འགའ་ཞིག་གི །

Therefore, the <term>Vedas</term> <gloss>ancient Hindu scriptures</gloss> also have a creator, because they are a source of valid knowledge <note>original: "pramana"</note>, just like the works of <term>Kumara</term> <gloss>referring to Kumarila or similar young authors</gloss> and others. As for how this pervasion <note>the logical necessity between being a source of knowledge and having a creator</note> works, it is stated as the manner of whichever category arises from whichever cause.

Specific qualities of power, such as being difficult to articulate or difficult to hear, or the ability to neutralize poison and so forth, as well as the function of revealing hidden objects that transcend the senses—all these different categories should be examined as common to all <note>meaning these qualities are found in human compositions as well as scriptures</note>. In consideration of this, it is said that there is no distinction from them; that is, there is no distinction from the <term>Vedas</term>. Since this is the case, and because there is no valid proof for the definite reliability of individual words, one should not think that the authority of the <term>Vedas</term> alone is to be accepted as valid.

The statement because it was made by a person expresses the doubt of the opponent. The scriptures of <term>Vishnu</term> <gloss>Puranic or Vaishnava texts</gloss> and others are well known to have been made by a person. This implies that they contradict the claim that scripture is not man-made <note>original: "apauruseya"</note>. The section beginning with The person is a refutation. 

One cannot say that the <term>Vedas</term> are not made by a person simply because a creator is not perceived. Because a very long time has passed and the origins transcend the senses, the inability to observe a creator does not allow one to negate the existence of a creator. Therefore, the very absence of a creator is subject to doubt. For this reason, the fact that something was made by a person does not serve as a refutation of the claim that it was not made by a person. From what valid source of knowledge <note>original: "pramana"</note> does this claim come? The meaning is that no such valid source of knowledge exists. 

This debate was elaborated upon in the first chapter, and is only briefly mentioned here as the occasion demands. The statement or else expresses an alternative position. The phrase those words refers to those which are well known to have a creator. If one wonders whether there is any observed error where someone thinks "I made this" regarding something they did not actually make, it is addressed in the section beginning with In this way. For some who are prone to conceit...

It would have been sufficient to mention the activity, but why is it necessary to mention the <term>dhatu</term> <gloss>element/domain</gloss>? If only the earth were mentioned, then even the white and red substances derived from the elements would be referred to by the world <note>the common worldly designation</note> as such. To prevent such confusion, the word <term>dhatu</term> <gloss>element</gloss> is used. To summarize and demonstrate what was explained above, the text says: what this form is, and so on. When this form, characterized by the four great elements, and the four formless aggregates of name explained above are gathered together, they are called <term>namarupa</term> <gloss>name and form</gloss>.

According to the <term>Abhidharma</term> <gloss>Higher Knowledge/Phenomenology</gloss>, form is of three types:
1. Visible and obstructive.
2. Invisible and obstructive.
3. Invisible and non-obstructive.

Name is also of three types: the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formation, excluding the aggregate of consciousness. These three types of form and three types of name, when gathered together, are called name and form. Regarding these, visible and obstructive form is established as that which is the object of the eye faculty, known as form. Invisible and obstructive form consists of nine substances: the five faculties such as the eye, and the four objects of sound, smell, taste, and touch. Invisible and non-obstructive form is <term>avijnapti-rupa</term> <gloss>unmanifest form</gloss>.

To demonstrate the six sense bases, the text says: the name which, conditioned by form, is called the six sense bases, and so on. There are precisely six sense bases. To show the distinct divisions of the six sense bases by name, it says: the eye sense base, and so on. Among these, from the cause of the form of the four great elements, the sense bases from the eye sense base up to the body sense base arise. From the cause of the four aggregates of name, the mind sense base arises. Alternatively, when the four great elements become pure and clear, they become the eye sense base through the body sense base.

<summary>This page explains the technical definitions of Name and Form and the Six Sense Bases within Buddhist phenomenology. It categorizes physical form into three types based on visibility and resistance while defining the causal relationships between the elements and the sensory organs.</summary>
<keywords>Namarupa, Abhidharma, Four Great Elements, Six Sense Bases, Ayatana, Unmanifest Form, Aggregates</keywords>

The text says: "If it possesses five factors <note>Sanskrit: aṅga</note>, the act of killing is complete. If any of these are missing, it is not considered the full act of killing."

To show the first factor, it says: "It must be a living being." The victim must actually be a sentient being <term>sattva</term> <gloss>a living creature</gloss>, and not something like a pillar or a tree stump.

To show the second factor, it says: "One must have the perception of it as a living being." If one intends to kill a specific being and knows it is a living being, the act of killing occurs. However, if one strikes a living being while perceiving it as a tree stump or something else, the act <note>of intentional killing</note> is not fulfilled. In short, this means that the very being one intended to kill must be the one killed, without mistake.

To show the third factor, it says: "The intent to kill must have arisen." If one kills with the motivated thought, "I shall kill," then it is the act of killing. If there is no intent to kill—that is, if one kills with a mind free of afflictive emotions <term>kleśa</term>—it is not considered the act of killing.

To show the fourth factor, it says: "An injury must be inflicted." Even if there is an intent to kill, if one does not strike with a weapon or similar means, it is not the act of killing. The meaning is that one must actually strike with a weapon or other method due to the intent to kill.

To show the fifth factor, it says: "The victim must die." When the continuity of the life faculty <term>jīvitendriya</term> <gloss>the force that sustains life</gloss> of the victim is severed and they die, all five factors are complete, and the act of killing is finalized.

Regarding the phrase "cutting life," life refers to the life faculty. To harm or stop its continuity is "killing." Even at the very end of a lifespan, if one creates an obstacle to the arising of even a single moment of the life faculty that was yet to come, it is considered the act of killing.

<summary>This page defines the five specific conditions required for the act of killing to be karmically complete according to Buddhist monastic and ethical theory. It emphasizes the roles of intent, correct identification of the victim, and the actual cessation of the life faculty.</summary>
<keywords>killing, five factors, ethics, life faculty, intent, Vinaya, sentient beings</keywords>

When requesting <term>pravrajya</term> <gloss>monastic ordination</gloss>, the bodhisattva generates the mind of enlightenment, thinking: May all sentient beings become characterized by the dharma that is free from obstacles and irreversible.

When discarding white clothes <note>referring to the transition from lay life to monastic life</note>, the bodhisattva generates the mind of enlightenment, thinking: May all sentient beings abandon the pursuit of negativity and become thoroughly purified in the roots of virtue.

When shaving the hair and beard, the bodhisattva generates the mind of enlightenment, thinking: May all sentient beings become perfectly meditative and free from <term>kleshas</term> <gloss>disturbing emotions</gloss>.

When donning saffron robes, the bodhisattva generates the mind of enlightenment, thinking: May all sentient beings possess the mind of a great <term>rishi</term> <gloss>sage</gloss> and be free from impurity.

At the time of ordaining, the bodhisattva generates the mind of enlightenment, thinking: For the sake of protecting all sentient beings, may they ordain with the ordination of a <term>Tathagata</term> <gloss>Buddha</gloss>.

When taking refuge in the Buddha, the bodhisattva generates the mind of enlightenment, thinking: Having developed a clear aspiration for virtue, may all sentient beings strive to ensure that the lineage of the Buddha is never interrupted.

When taking refuge in the Dharma, the bodhisattva generates the mind of enlightenment, thinking: May all sentient beings hear the treasury of the Dharma.

When taking refuge in the <term>Sangha</term> <gloss>spiritual community</gloss>, the bodhisattva generates the mind of enlightenment, thinking: May all sentient beings be free from the state of attachment and perfectly gather the Sangha together.

When purely adopting the words of training <note>the monastic vows or precepts</note>, the bodhisattva generates the mind of enlightenment, thinking: May all sentient beings act purely with excellent conduct and be thoroughly trained in all the trainings.

གང་གི་ཕྱིར། །བྱང་ཕྱོགས་སུ་ནི་འགྲོ་བ་ན། །གང་དག་ཕྱོགས་དེར་གནས་པ་ཡི། །རྒྱུ་སྐར་ཁྱོད་ལ་སྐྱོང་གྱུར་ཅིག །མོན་གྲུ་དང་ནི་མོན་གྲེ་དང་། །ཁྲུམས་སྟོད་དང་ནི་ཁྲུམས་སྨད་དང་། །ནམ་གྲུ་དང་ནི་ཐ་སྐར་དང་། །བྲ་ཉེ་སྟེ་ནི་བདུན་པོ་ཡིན། །རྒྱུ་སྐར་བདུན་པོ་དེ་དག་ནི། །འཇིག་རྟེན་སྐྱོང་བར་

May it be auspicious! He has many sons, wise and with names that match one another. There are ninety-one of them in total, great and powerful, all known by the name Indra <note>In this context, Indra refers to a class of powerful celestial beings or sons of the guardian kings</note>. May they grant you freedom from disease and protect you with great excellence.

In the direction of the western quarter, there are eight youthful goddesses: <term>Karnamdhara</term> <gloss>Earring-wearer</gloss>, <term>Keshini</term> <gloss>Fine-haired</gloss>, <term>Pundarika</term> <gloss>White Lotus</gloss>, <term>Aruna</term> <gloss>Dawn</gloss>, <term>Amati</term> <gloss>Infinite</gloss>, <term>Navama</term> <gloss>Ninth</gloss>, <term>Lila</term> <gloss>Playful</gloss>, and <term>Krishna</term> <gloss>Dark One</gloss>, along with <term>Chavega</term> <gloss>Swift Pace</gloss>. May they grant you freedom from disease and protect you with great excellence.

In the direction of the western quarter, there is a mountain called the West. There, both the sun and moon set. May that setting also bestow wealth upon you. May it grant you freedom from disease and protect you with great excellence. May you find peace in every direction. May you not fall into sin. Having been thoroughly protected by all the gods, may you find wealth and return safely.

For whatever purpose you travel toward the northern direction, may the constellations dwelling in that quarter protect you. They are the seven: <term>Abhijit</term> <gloss>Victorious</gloss>, <term>Shravana</term> <gloss>Hearing</gloss>, <term>Purvabhadrapada</term> <gloss>Former Auspicious Foot</gloss>, <term>Uttarabhadrapada</term> <gloss>Latter Auspicious Foot</gloss>, <term>Revati</term> <gloss>Wealthy</gloss>, <term>Ashvini</term> <gloss>Horse-tamer</gloss>, and <term>Bharani</term> <gloss>Bearing</gloss>. These seven constellations are famous as world-protectors. It is taught that they reside in the northern direction. May they protect you at all times.

Their lord and king is <term>Vaishravana</term> <gloss>Son of Vishrava</gloss>, who rides upon a man and has a misshapen body <note>referring to his epithet Kubera, often depicted as stout or physically unique</note>. He is the master of all <term>yakshas</term> <gloss>nature spirits</gloss>. May he, along with <term>Dhanabhadra</term> <gloss>Excellent Wealth</gloss>, protect you. He has many sons, wise and with names that match one another. There are ninety-one of them in total, great and powerful, all known by the name Indra. May they grant you freedom from disease and protect you with great excellence.

In the direction of the northern quarter, there are eight youthful goddesses: <term>Atirakta</term> <gloss>Deeply Attached</gloss>, <term>Sahasradevi</term> <gloss>Thousand-Goddess</gloss>, <term>Prithivi</term> <gloss>Earth</gloss>, and likewise <term>Padmini</term> <gloss>Lotus-like</gloss>, <term>Upasthayika</term> <gloss>Attendant to the Great King</gloss>, <term>Parvati</term> <gloss>Mountain Daughter</gloss>, <term>Hri</term> <gloss>Modesty</gloss>, and <term>Shri</term> <gloss>Glorious One</gloss>. May they grant you freedom from disease and protect you with great excellence.

In the direction of the northern quarter, there is a mountain possessed of fragrant scents <note>Gandhamadana</note>. It is the dwelling place of <term>yakshas</term> and elemental spirits, and goddesses of various beautiful forms. May they also grant you freedom from disease.

<summary>This page contains protective verses and invocations to the deities of the western and northern quarters, including lists of goddesses, constellations, and the king Vaishravana. These prayers are intended to ensure the health, safety, and success of travelers seeking wealth.</summary>

<keywords>Vaishravana, northern direction, western direction, constellations, nakshatra, yaksha, protective deities, Indra, Buddhist protection rituals</keywords>

For example, suppose a person sets out through a great wilderness and is afflicted by hunger and thirst. In search of food, they climb a tree of great fruit. However, without tasting the fruit of excellent scent and excellent flavor, they abandon that tree of great fruit and climb a poison tree. Having eaten the fruit of the poison tree, they meet their death. It is said that such a person is just like that.

Though they found the human state that is difficult to find, and having found it, desired to enter the <term>Mahayana</term> <gloss>Great Vehicle</gloss> by relying on a <term>kalyanamitra</term> <gloss>spiritual friend</gloss>, they instead praised themselves and disparaged others for the sake of profit and honor. Thus, a heavy downfall such as this arises. Because of that heavy downfall, they are despised by all the wise and will go to the lower realms. Such a person is not to be relied upon by anyone of the royal caste, the priestly caste, the merchant caste, or the commoner caste. Anyone who relies upon them will be abandoned by all the wise. This is the sixth root downfall of a beginner <term>Bodhisattva</term> <gloss>enlightenment being</gloss>.

Furthermore, son of noble family, in the future there will appear royal chaplains who are outcasts, ministers who are outcasts, hunters who are outcasts, and ministers possessing the pride of the wise who have great wealth and great enjoyments. These people will appear to engage in many kinds of meritorious deeds arising from generosity. Yet, intoxicated and arrogant because of their giving, they will harbor pride and haughtiness. They will create schisms that divide the royalty and the <term>shramanas</term> <gloss>ascetic practitioners</gloss>, and divide the royalty themselves. Relying on their royal status, they will cause the <term>shramanas</term> to be punished and cause their wealth to be seized through punishment. Due to that harm, they will cause those <term>shramanas</term> to steal what belongs to individuals, to the local community of monks, to the community of the four directions, or to the <term>stupas</term> <gloss>relic monuments</gloss>, and will then offer those things as bribes. Those outcasts will then offer these to the royalty.

<summary>This page defines the sixth root downfall for beginner Bodhisattvas, which involves self-praise and the disparagement of others for personal gain. It also warns of future corruption where wealthy officials and outcasts will cause conflict between the state and the monastic community, leading to the theft of religious property.</summary>
<keywords>Mahayana, Bodhisattva, root downfall, ethics, pride, monastic property, social castes, corruption</keywords>

Homage to the Tathagata, the Arhat <gloss>Foe Destroyer</gloss>, the Perfectly Complete Buddha, the King of the Lord of Mountains who is firmly seated upon a Jewel Lotus.

May all those Buddhas and Bhagavan <gloss>Blessed Lords</gloss> who reside, live, and remain throughout all the world systems of the universe, and however many Tathagatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Complete Buddhas there may be, please turn your attention toward me.

In this life and in other lives, throughout the cycle of existence from beginningless births until now, whatever sinful actions I have committed, or caused others to commit, or rejoiced in others committing; whatever wealth belonging to stupas <gloss>relic monuments</gloss>, wealth belonging to the Sangha <gloss>monastic community</gloss>, or wealth belonging to the Sangha of the four directions I have stolen, caused to be stolen, or rejoiced in the stealing of; whatever inexpiable actions <note>referring to the five heinous crimes</note> I have committed, or caused others to commit, or rejoiced in the committing of; whatever paths of the ten non-virtuous actions I have engaged in, or caused others to engage in, or rejoiced in the engagement of; whatever karmic obscurations I am obscured by, because of which sentient beings are reborn in hells…

By preceded by the application of correctly gathering the teachings, and in order to achieve all things simultaneously, the third great aspiration is accomplished. This aspiration is as vast as the limits of the <term>dharmadhātu</term> <gloss>sphere of reality</gloss>, extending to the edges of the realm of space, reaching to the very end of future time, and proceeding continuously before all the Buddhas who appear throughout the counting of eons.

It is as follows: in order to accomplish the generation of a stable mind by granting instructions and advice for purifying the <term>pāramitās</term> <gloss>perfections</gloss>, which reveal all the paths of the <term>bhūmis</term> <gloss>levels of realization</gloss> belonging to the conduct of a Bodhisattva. This conduct is extremely extensive, great, immeasurable, and indivisible. It is comprised of all the perfections, the complete purification of the levels, and the accomplishment of the primary and secondary branches. It includes the conduct of a Bodhisattva with similar and dissimilar characteristics, as well as their condensation and expansion. Thus, the fourth great aspiration is accomplished: to continuously manifest throughout all the countings of eons of practice, as vast as the sphere of reality, extending to the edges of the realm of space, and reaching to the very end of future time.

It is as follows: for the sake of ripening all beings without exception—whether they have form or are formless, whether they have perception, lack perception, or are neither with nor without perception; whether they are born from an egg, born from a womb, born from warmth and moisture, or born miraculously; those belonging to the three realms, those included in the six migrations, and those belonging to every type of birth—all beings comprised of name and form. To engage them in the teachings of the Buddha, to cut through all their worldly migrations, and to establish them in the wisdom of omniscience, the fifth great aspiration is made. One must hold the actions of the three doors <note>referring to the three doors of body, speech, and mind</note> with mindfulness. Abandoning faults, accomplish what is good and meaningful. Do not engage in meaningless behavior. Always cultivate your own good qualities. Regarding the application of the virtuous side, be enthusiastic and do not let your mind become discouraged or lifeless. Seek out friends who abandon negativity and increase good qualities; hold them in your mind with harmony. Pay respectful homage to those possessing good qualities.

Through skillful means, abandon the afflictions <term>klesha</term> <gloss>mental obscurations such as attachment, anger, and ignorance</gloss> of living beings. Toward all friends, whether high or low, act like one extracting milk from water; discard the faults and take up the virtues. Be grateful for what has been done for you and repay the kindness. Do not create conditions for others to sin, and do not create obstacles to virtue.

Do not be jealous of the prosperity of those in high positions. Toward friends and those of lower status, do not act with contempt or engage in belittling them. Proclaim your own faults and the virtues of others. Do not speak of others' faults and do not praise yourself. Considering the future life as more important than this one, let all your actions be in accord with the Dharma <gloss>the Buddha's teachings and the natural law of virtue</gloss>.

Abandon the material things of this life and adorn the body with the riches of the Noble Ones <note>the seven riches of the Aryas: faith, ethics, learning, generosity, integrity, consideration, and wisdom</note>. Do not mistake sufferings for happiness. Abandoning sleep, dullness, laziness, and distraction, develop the recognition of the certainty of death. Even if a virtue is small, accomplish it with effort. Even if a sin is small, abandon it completely.

Except for the sake of the Dharma, do not strive for food, clothing, and the like. Have little desire and practice contentment. Completely abandon the eight worldly concerns <note>gain and loss, pleasure and pain, praise and blame, fame and insignificance</note>. Do not engage in flattery or hinting for gain. Without noticing your own faults, do not examine the faults of others. Abandon the habit of making brave promises out of a love for talking and then failing to act accordingly.

Do not practice deceit or pretense, and completely abandon wrong livelihoods. Accomplish your goals in accordance with the Dharma. Do not be attached or clinging toward relatives and relations; be without bias or partiality. Have little expectation of others. Do not praise non-virtuous actions, but disparage them. Abandon unnecessary busyness and do not take pleasure in idle gossip; thus, block the yearning of desire. Abandon discouragement and shame regarding actions that gain qualities and increase the accumulation of merit. Subdue pride and arrogance with their antidotes. Malice and haughtiness…
